content: The shortnose sturgeon, scientifically known as Acipenser brevirostrum, is a small sturgeon species native to North America. It inhabits 16 to 19 large river and estuary systems along the Atlantic seaboard, ranging from the Saint John River in New Brunswick, Canada, to the St. Johns River in Florida, United States. Evidence suggests that populations of this species may be disjunct, as there are few records of individuals in the sea outside the influence of their home rivers, and tagged individuals are rarely captured outside the rivers where they were tagged. The species has been found in salinities up to 30-31 parts per thousand, which is slightly below the salinity of seawater. The shortnose sturgeon is classified as an endangered species in the United States, a status it has held since 1967, and is considered a vulnerable species in Canada. Adults of this species are often mistaken for juvenile Atlantic sturgeon due to their similar size. Historical commercial fishing records did not differentiate between the two species, with both being reported as common sturgeon. However, based on size data, it is believed that most of the catch consisted of Atlantic sturgeon. Shortnose sturgeon spawn in freshwater, above the tidal head, in areas with moving water over rubble or gravel bottoms that have minimal silt or organic material. Spawning occurs at water temperatures between 5 and 15 degrees Celsius. The timing of spawning varies by location, occurring as early as January in South Carolina or Georgia and as late as May in Maine and New Brunswick. Eggs hatch after 13 days, producing hatchlings that are 7-11 mm long. These hatchlings have a large yolk sac, limited vision, minimal swimming ability, and a strong tendency to seek cover. After another 9-12 days, they develop into swimming larvae approximately 15 mm in length. By the time they reach 20 mm, they resemble miniature adults and begin feeding. The larvae drift downstream in the deep channels of the river and remain in freshwater for the first year of life. Juveniles, which can grow up to 18 inches in length, typically move to areas where freshwater and saltwater mix, following the tidal cycle. Adults can be found in both freshwater and saltwater environments. Sexual maturity is reached at lengths of 45-55 cm (18-22 inches), with the age of maturity varying by latitude. Males mature earlier, at 2-3 years in Georgia and 10-14 years in New Brunswick, while females mature between 6 and 17 years of age, with earlier maturity occurring in southern rivers. First spawning occurs 1-2 years after sexual maturity for males and up to 5 years later for females. Adults continue to grow, reaching lengths of 3-4 feet. Males may breed annually or biennially and rarely live beyond 30 years. Females typically breed every 3-5 years, laying between 40,000 and 200,000 eggs during spawning years, and can live up to 67 years. Females experience reduced feeding and growth for several years while producing gonadal material for spawning. It is hypothesized, though not conclusively proven, that maximum ages are lower in southern populations and higher in northern populations. In some locations, such as the Connecticut River in Massachusetts, the Santee River in South Carolina, and the Saint John River in New Brunswick, shortnose sturgeon have survived as landlocked populations following the construction of river dams. This indicates that the species does not require saltwater for its life cycle. Northern populations tend to spend more time in saltwater than southern populations, with some northern populations exhibiting an anadromous life cycle, while southern populations are more amphidromous. Shortnose sturgeon are bottom feeders, primarily consuming insects and small crustaceans. Juveniles have been observed with stomach contents containing up to 90% non-food items, suggesting they may randomly vacuum the river bottom. Adults in freshwater primarily feed on mollusks, while in estuaries, their diet includes polychaetes and small benthic fish. In freshwater, they also consume crustaceans and insects. The largest population of shortnose sturgeon, estimated at over 38,000 adults, is found in the Hudson River. The second-largest population, with 18,000 adults and approximately 100,000 individuals of all ages, resides in the Saint John River. Non-human predation on shortnose sturgeon is minimal. Yellow perch have been found with young sturgeon in their stomachs, and it is believed that sharks and seals may occasionally prey on adults. Parasites are not considered harmful to this species, and there are no reported cases of diseases among wild shortnose sturgeon. However, one hatchery population has experienced a disease outbreak. Genetically, shortnose sturgeon are 16-ploid, meaning their chromosomes are grouped in sets of 16 rather than pairs, as is typical for most vertebrates. It is thought that the shortnose sturgeon may have been one of the last sturgeon species to evolve.
